entries.english: The Three Taita Hills Dialect Varieties (Wray 1894 & Johnston 1919 #14–15)
entries.context: Rev. J. A. Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language' & Sir Harry H. Johnston (1919, Vol. I, pp. 82–93)

entries.english: 9 Noun Classes & Concord System in Kisagala (Wray 1894, pp. 9–13)
entries.translation: Cl. I m-/wa- (mundu/wandu) • Cl. II m-/mi- (mgunda/migunda, mwiti/mīti) • Cl. III n-/n- (nyumba, mbuzi) • Cl. IV ki-,cha-/vi-,va- (kituli/vituli, chala/vala) • Cl. V i-,u-/ma-,mau- (iwano/mawano, ulili/maulili, meji) • Cl. VI lu-/nyu- (lumbo/nyumbo) • Cl. VII ka-,tu-/vi- Diminutives (kanyumba/vinyumba, tunguku/vinguku) • Cl. VIII andu (place, kwa-) • Cl. IX ku- Infinitives (kugora kwako)
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', pp. 9–13

entries.english: Class VII Diminutives (ka- & tu- sg. → vi- pl. in Wray 1894, pp. 12–13; ka-/tu- in Johnston 1919 #15)
entries.translation: kanyumba → pl. vinyumba (little house), tunguku → pl. vinguku (little fowl), tumwana → pl. viwana (little child); Kidawida: kanyonyi → tunyonyi (little bird), kachi → tuchi (little brook)
entries.pronunciation: ka-nyum-ba / vi-nyum-ba, tu-ngu-ku / vi-ngu-ku, tu-mwa-na / vi-wa-na
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894, pp. 12–13) Kisagala Class VII & Sir Harry Johnston (1919, #15) Kidawida

entries.english: Locative Case Suffix -eni / -ni with kwa- Concord (Wray 1894, p. 13)
entries.translation: nyumba → nyumbeni kwangu (in my house), mbua → mbueni (in the garden), boro → boroni (in the cattle-fold), ngileni kwake (in his way), chongoni kwetu (in our heads)
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', p. 13

entries.english: 7 Derivative Verb Forms in Kisagala (Wray 1894, pp. 60–62)
entries.translation: 1. Frequentative (-na-...-a'ga: tana-dea'ga, wana-lima'ga) • 2. Applied (-ila/-ela: kudeila, kulimila, kuletela) • 3. Causative (-isa/-isha/-sa: kududugisha, kugalisha, kuujisa) • 4. Neuter/Feasible (-ka/-ika/-oka: kuvunjika, kugoloka, kudeika, kukamika) • 5. Reflexive (-ku-...-ēn: naku-kwita mwēn) • 6. Reciprocal (-ana/-anya: kushaiana, kulwanana, kugendanya) • 7. Strengthened/Reduplicated (kupasa-pasa, kuhada-hada)
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', pp. 60–62

entries.english: 12 Ideophonic Adverbial Enclitics in Kisagala (Wray 1894, pp. 75–76)
entries.translation: Nyamala chwi (dead silent) • Ikumi chululu (ten and only ten) • Chanuka buu (smells horridly) • Mkundu lu (bright red) • Onyilu pi/fi (jet black) • Omnyangi tse (snow white) • Chakesua doo (fading red/yellow) • Nagora go (said everything) • Chanakulile ku (very hard) • Chamanga tuku (very fast/firm) • Chaoma ng'we ng'a (bone dry) • Si-shaia ng'o (not at all)
entries.pronunciation: nyamala chwi / ikumi chululu / mkundu lu / onyilu pi / omnyangi tse / chaoma ng'we ng'a
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', pp. 75–76

entries.english: Taita Proverb #665 Recorded by Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891, p. 160): Two occupations were too heavy for the hyena
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) 'African Aphorisms; or, Saws from Swahili-Land', Taita Proverb § 665, p. 160

entries.english: Traditional Taita Riddle (Enigma) Formula (Wray 1894, p. 93): My house has no door?
entries.translation: Wada! — Resp.: Na wada! — Riddle: Nyumba yangu siiwesi mjango? — If unguessed: Ni-hawe muzi ('Give me a town') — Answer: Igi ('An egg')
entries.pronunciation: wa-da! na wa-da! nyum-ba yan-gu si-i-we-si m-jan-go? ni-ha-we mu-zi — i-gi
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', p. 93 (Enigma)

entries.english: 4 Taita Seasons & Coldest Months (Wray 1894, p. 113 & p. 116)
entries.translation: Ishika (mvula ya ishika, March–May greater rains) • Kwalazi (June–Sept cold dry season; June–July = Mtsuo) • Vuli (mvula ya vuli, Oct–Dec lesser rains) • Kaskazi (Jan–Feb hot season)
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', p. 113 (Rain) & p. 116 (Season)

entries.english: 13 Taita Divisions of Day & Night and Lunar Decades (Wray 1894, p. 106 & p. 123)
entries.translation: makeo (1st cock-crow), ikesho kiro (2nd cock-crow), ikesho (sunrise), msenya (daytime), msenya 'gati (midday), ijua ku-chunguluka (past noon), hafuka (afternoon/evening), lumisimisi (dusk), kiro (night), nyungu ku-kalla motoni (~9 p.m. 'pot on the fire'), wandu ku-tungura (10–11 p.m. 'people dozing'), haring'a za hambiri (12–2 a.m. 'first sleep'), haring'a za nyuma (3–4 a.m. 'last sleep') • Lunar decades: mwezi kongo (new moon), ikumi lya hambiri, ikumi lya 'gati, ikumi lya kizimu
entries.pronunciation: ma-ke-o / i-ke-sho / m-se-nya ga-ti / ha-fu-ka / lu-mi-si-mi-si / ha-rin-ga za ham-bi-ri
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', p. 106 (Month) & p. 123 (Time)

entries.english: 9 Stages of Maize (ibemba) & 9 Stages of Sorghum (mwemba) Growth (Wray 1894, pp. 87–88)
entries.translation: Maize (ibemba/mabemba): 1. ku-oka (sprout), 2. koka (blade), 3. mchokochoko, 4. mwakolola, 5. mwatumbulua, 6. mwavala, 7. mwatunga (forming grain), 8. mwabala, 9. mwaoma (ripe) • Sorghum (mwemba): 1. ku-mera, 2. mwakumbania, 3. mwaguta (hollow stem), 4. mwatunga mimba, 5. mwabuta (ear comes out), 6. mwaalika, 7. mwatunga, 8. mwakomaa, 9. mwaoma
entries.pronunciation: i-bem-ba / ma-bem-ba / m-cho-ko-cho-ko / mwem-ba / mwa-gu-ta / mwa-o-ma
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', pp. 87–88 (Corn)

entries.english: 11 Taita Antelope Species & Bush-Buck Bathing Taboo (Wray 1894, pp. 79, 84, 109, 113)
entries.translation: sambe (male kudu) & i'galu (female kudu), shakwa (water-buck), makuli (small yellow antelope), isha (steinbok), mbala (gazelle), ngulungu (bush-buck — taboo against washing in streams, p. 84), dom (eland), gwali (hartebeest), nausi (impala), tamahi (oryx, p. 109), ndoli (reed-buck, p. 113)
entries.pronunciation: sam-be / i-ga-lu / sha-kwa / ngu-lu-ngu / dom / gwa-li / na-u-si / ta-ma-hi
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', pp. 79, 84, 109, 113

entries.english: Ivory Tusk Trade Grades, Beads & Cloth Varieties (Wray 1894, pp. 81, 86, 102)
entries.translation: Ivory (njovu, p. 102): kibori (very small tusk), tofwa (small), tofwa shagangi (medium), isange (largest prime tusk) • Beads (lukangi/ngangi, p. 81): maziwa (large white), njama (small red), kanyera, kikoromba, mtinikia, ngolole, mbuibui, kipundurya, kisambe • Cloth (nguwo, p. 86): ilesi, kaniki, bafuta, mardufu, kanga, kikoi, shuka, ibusha, kitambi
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', pp. 81, 86, 102

entries.english: Traditional Musical Instruments & Taita War-Cry (Wray 1894, p. 89 & p. 107)
entries.translation: Instruments (p. 107): ngoma (drum), gunda (horn), nderere (flute), nguli (small dance bells), mbewewe (ankle rattles) • War-cry (lukungu, p. 89): 'Mwasasi, mwasasi wome, mwana wa ng'anya mbareni ngolo, mwasasi wome!'
entries.pronunciation: ngo-ma / gun-da / nde-re-re / ngu-li / m-be-we-we / lu-kun-gu
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', p. 89 (Cry) & p. 107 (Musical instruments)

entries.english: Reciprocal Grandparent/Grandchild Kinship, Ancestral Skull Caves & Ancient Cairns (Wray 1894, pp. 81, 84, 98, 99, 118, 124)
entries.translation: wawa (grandfather/grandson reciprocal) & ake (grandmother/granddaughter reciprocal, p. 98) • ngoma / ngomeni (ancestral spirits & sacred skull caves where skulls of elders were preserved after about a year, pp. 84, 118) • mfingiri (ancient stone cairns built by the aboriginal Warwana, p. 99) & Mwibabu (ancient aboriginal people who made red earthenware pots with ears, pp. 81, 124)
entries.pronunciation: wa-wa / a-ke / ngo-ma / ngo-me-ni / m-fin-gi-ri / wa-rwa-na / mwi-ba-bu
entries.context: Rev. J. Alfred Wray (1894) 'An Elementary Introduction to the Taita Language', pp. 81, 84, 98, 99, 118, 124

entries.english: Sir Harry Johnston's (1919–1922) #14 Taita (Ki-dabida, Ki-sagala, Ki-siγau) Comparative Corpus
entries.translation: Three Dialects (Vol. I, p. 112 & Vol. II, pp. 32–33): Ki-dabida (Dabida/Bura hills), Ki-sagala (Sagala hills), and Ki-siγau (Mount Kasiγau; in Ki-siγau v replaces w/b, γ stands for g, z for s, d for t, and r for older z) • Pronouns & Particles (pp. 107–110): 1s I-mi/Mīmi (poss. -āpō/-āpwa 'my'), 1p I-swi/I-su (Dū-/Tū-, poss. -ēdū/-ētū 'our'), 3p I-vō/Wāō (Vā-/Wā-, poss. -āvō/-āwō 'their'), -ōsē/-pūtū ('all'), Śi-kātī ('middle'), -a n-dēnyi ('inside', Errata p. x), Ā-ā!/Ndē! ('no!'), negative verb prefixes Ndē-, Sī-, Tā- • Distinctive Roots (pp. 98–106 & Vol. II, p. 33): I-rawa/M-riω/I-vi (arrow), I-fuwe/I-sabaω (baboon), Baga/Bi-gati (blood), N-dana (bow), Sukω/M-zoṅgω (brains), Lagaya/Ki-kua (man's breast), M-zuri/M-fumwa (chief), I-saṅga (country), N-tagω (heifer), Ki-lavu/M-si/I-dime (day), Kωši/Kωci/Cucu (dog), M-ωdω (fire, Errata p. x), Lu-aiyω pl. ny-aiyω (foot, Errata p. x), Ōrω/Hōrω/M-fωgω/Fwandi (he-goat), M-beni/M-buguma (she-goat), C-oṅgω pl. vy-oṅgω (head), Ki-fumvu/Fumbu/M-gondi (hill/mountain), M-garω (bachelors' hut), Mw-ēda/M-ωda (river), I-dīme (today), Mā-zīndē/Kēlω (tomorrow), I-gōlω (yesterday), Fōrω (zebra)
entries.context: Sir Harry H. Johnston, 'A Comparative Study of the Bantu and Semi-Bantu Languages' (Vol. I, 1919, pp. 98–112; Vol. II, 1922, pp. 32–33)

entries.english: Dr. Krapf's (1850, pp. v–vi) Wateita of Kadiáro, Ndara & Bura and the Ethnonym "Ambakómo"
entries.translation: In his Preface dated October 14, 1850 (pp. v–vi), Rev. Dr. J. L. Krapf records collecting a vocabulary of the Wateita language and documents that the Wateita of the mountains of Kadiáro (Kasigau), Ndara (Sagala), and Bura (Dabida) call the coastal Wanika "Ambakómo" — preserving the historical memory that the ancestors of the Wanika formerly dwelt in the Pokómo country along the Tana River before being driven south by the Galla.
entries.context: Rev. Dr. J. L. Krapf (1850) 'Vocabulary of Six East-African Languages' (Tübingen), Preface pp. v–vi

source: Public Domain Historical Lexicons (Krapf 1850, Shaw 1885, Taylor 1891, Wray 1894 & Johnston 1919)
